content: Respiratory therapy is recognized as an allied health profession in both the United States and Canada. Professionals in this field, known as respiratory therapists (RTs) or respiratory care practitioners (RCPs), are experts in diagnosing and treating respiratory and cardiovascular conditions. These conditions include chronic diseases such as asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), as well as acute, multi-systemic complications arising from events like heart attacks, strokes, trauma, or complications during childbirth. RTs are highly skilled in airway management, mechanical ventilation, blood acid-base balance, and critical care medicine. They collaborate closely with other healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, speech therapists, and physical therapists. Over the past four decades, respiratory therapy has undergone significant development. Initially, respiratory therapists were on-the-job-trained technicians with minimal formal education, primarily tasked with ensuring the safe use of oxygen. However, the introduction of mechanical ventilators, modern CPR techniques, and advanced airway care methods created a demand for more comprehensively trained practitioners. Today, respiratory therapists are college-educated professionals working in diverse healthcare settings. To become a registered respiratory therapist (RRT), individuals must complete at least a two-year associate degree program, though three-, four-, and five-year degree programs are also available. Some institutions offer advanced degrees, such as master's and PhD programs. After completing their education, graduates must pass a national examination administered by the Canadian Board of Respiratory Care (CBRC) in Canada or the National Board for Respiratory Care (NBRC) in the United States. In the U.S., a two-tiered certification system exists: passing the initial certification exam grants the title of Certified Respiratory Therapist (CRT), while passing the registry exam confers the designation of Registered Respiratory Therapist (RRT). Additional specialization exams, such as those for neonatal/pediatric care, allow RTs to earn titles like CRT-NPS or RRT-NPS. Admission to respiratory therapy programs typically requires a strong academic background in science and mathematics, with grades of B+ or higher at the senior high school level. The curriculum includes courses in anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, pharmacology, chemistry, physics, microbiology, hemodynamics, mechanical ventilation, statistics, healthcare law, and medical ethics. These programs emphasize all body systems, with particular focus on the respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological, and renal systems. Class sizes are generally small, offering both classroom instruction and hands-on clinical experiences. Many applicants already hold science degrees. Due to the rigorous nature of the program, there is a measurable attrition rate, and most schools do not permit multiple rewrites of failed exams. Students must master, apply, and retain the material from the entire program, as there is no reliance on cookbook practices. RTs must think quickly under pressure and make critical life-or-death decisions. They serve as patient advocates and resources for staff, physicians, and patients, functioning as integral members of the healthcare team. Airway management is a primary skill for respiratory therapists, along with vascular access for intravenous lines, arterial lines, or arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling. RTs are essential members of Code Blue (cardiac arrest) teams. Some RTs receive specialized training to assist in operating rooms, high-risk deliveries, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and procedures like chest tube and central line insertion. In the homecare setting, RTs play a vital role, relying on clinical assessments and experience-based decision-making due to limited technical resources. This environment tests the full extent of an RT's knowledge and expertise. The education of RTs allows for continuous skill advancement and the acquisition of more advanced procedures. RTs typically act on physician orders, except in emergencies or when written protocols are in place. For example, at Duke University Medical Center, RTs handle all out-of-operating-room intubations. In Ontario, Canada, RTs intubate during in-hospital cardiac arrests and adjust ventilator settings based on their interpretation of blood gas results, often under physician orders such as ventilate according to respiratory therapist or adjust ventilator to maintain specific physiological values. These responsibilities require RTs to interpret lab results, assess patients, and make critical decisions, as errors could result in severe harm or death. RTs must be thoroughly educated and trained to perform these tasks safely. Additionally, they may conduct medical research projects. In the United States, respiratory therapy is regulated at the state level. Some states require licensure, while others accept accreditation from the NBRC. The American Association for Respiratory Care (AARC) is the primary professional organization for respiratory care providers in the U.S. In Canada, starting salaries for staff RRTs range from $40,000 in Prince Edward Island to $65,000 in Alberta. RTs typically receive four weeks of vacation after one year of employment, along with 11 statutory holidays. They can supplement their income through overtime work and continuing education opportunities.
